title: Bar Graph

illustrates.quote: A transcriber’s note provides information about how the information is presented.

blocks.text:
Change in Distribution of the
American Workforce, 1870-1920

figure.description: Two stacked bar graphs showing the distribution of the American workforce for the years 1870 and 1920. Each section of the bars represents a different industry, with a category label and percentage.

blocks.description: The data from print bar graphs is shown in a table. Numbers in the 1870 and 1920 columns are percentages.

print.notes: The book shows this same pair of bar graphs transcribed TWO valid ways per 6.11.3 ('Option 1: List Format' and 'Option 2: Table Format') — both option labels are the book's own print captions, not braille content, and are dropped here (matching the across-the-section convention). Only Option 2 (a genuine table, headers '1870'/'1920', one row per category) is modelled; Option 1 (a flat list per year, itself truncated after 'Trade' in the book's own excerpt with a '444' ellipsis — the remaining three categories are never shown for either year) is not separately tested here, to keep one file per original sample. Option 2's own row leader-dots (a proportional bar-length fill before each percentage, source-6.txt lines 5188-5195's own quote-mark/'3333' runs) are a graphical bar-length indicator with no plain-table equivalent — Emboss's table renderer has no bar-graph/proportional-fill mechanism at all (the tool's own header comment: 'a bar-graph derivation... is recorded per-sample instead of invented'); not built, and the resulting mismatch on those decorative cells is expected.
print.printFeatures: Two stacked bar graphs, one per year, broken into labelled percentage segments.

braille.notes: Table header row indented to line up over the value columns; each row's category name starts at cell 1, with a continuation line (for two-word categories) at cell 3. Row leader-dot bar-length fills omitted here (see print.notes) — the underlying percentage values themselves are kept.

resolution: Both runs conflated the book's own 'Option 1'/'Option 2' print captions and running-head furniture into braille.lines as literal English text, and both silently dropped the book's own '444' excerpt-ellipsis lines in Option 1 (source-6.txt lines 5168, 5173); this file's braille.lines were rebuilt from source-6.txt (lines 5179-5195, Option 2 only) directly, decoded with the same script used throughout this reconciliation. Every value/label confirmed by exact forward-translation (e.g. '10.4%' -> '#AJ4D.0', 'Professional, Clerical,' / 'Public Service', 'Manufacturing/' / 'Transportation' all reproduce their braille exactly, including the two-line wrap on the longer category names). print.blocks[2] (the actual table) was built here since neither run supplied one, only a flat figure.labels array with no row/column structure.
